text: Right now, your phone knows where you are, to within a few metres.
It works it out by listening
to ticking clocks.
About thirty satellites circle twenty thousand kilometres above us.
Each one carries an atomic clock,
and broadcasts the time, over and over.
The signal travels at the speed of light,
but it still arrives a little late.
And that delay is a distance.
One satellite puts you somewhere on a circle.
Two, at one of two points.
Three.
Right here.
But, there's a catch.
Up there, time itself runs at a different speed.
Moving fast slows the orbiting clock,
by seven microseconds a day.
Weaker gravity speeds it up, by forty-five.
Together, thirty-eight microseconds fast. Every single day.
Sounds tiny. But in thirty-eight microseconds,
light travels over eleven kilometres.
Left alone, your map pin would drift that far, every day.
By next week, you'd be somewhere out at sea.
So before launch, engineers tune the satellite clocks to tick slightly slow.
Einstein's relativity, quietly at work in your pocket.
